## Two kinds of aim {.smaller}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to understand**

- What reproducibility, robustness and replicability each mean
- What each tool of the toolchain does, and what none of them can do
- Why plain text, a script and a render step make an analysis checkable
- How a published file becomes the file that an analysis uses, and where errors enter
- What version control and an archive add to a finished analysis
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.small}
**What I want you to be able to do**

- Run R in the browser lab and, if you have installed it, in your IDE
- Read, filter, recode and summarise a data file with datawizard
- Reproduce a recorded result from the public file of a study
- Put that result in a Quarto report whose numbers come from the code
- Restart, run everything again and check that the numbers hold
:::
:::
::::

::: notes
Two columns, because the day has two kinds of aim. The left-hand column is conceptual, and today most of it is about what the tools are for rather than which one to pick: why a plain-text script and a render step make an analysis checkable, and where errors creep in between a published file and the numbers in a paper. The right-hand column is what you will have done by the end. You will have run R, read and recoded a real data file, reproduced a published result from it, and put that result into a report in which every number comes from the code. The case of the day, an experiment on housing authorities, is the material for all of this, and the reproduction is the target that the R work reaches in the afternoon.
:::
